This chapter states what the data currently shows, organized by research
question. Each question opens with a

section intended to stand
alone with the effects that answer the question, including estimates and inferential
support. Layers 2 and 3 qualify that answer in further detail, i.e. mechanism, moderators, boundary
conditions, limitations.

Inference is reported on the effect-size scale wherever possible. At the present
sample size, between-participant tests detect correlations of approximately
r >= 0.34; smaller effects are reported as estimates with uncertainty / descriptively.
The analysis set is substantially (enormously) larger than a paper could carry. The section

at the end is meant to designate which models are
load-bearing and which are supporting - to be discussed.

.
Deeper instruction produces large gains in accuracy,
defense performance (blocked mosquitos) and net placement concentration;
a single observed transition is propagated to a cue that was not yet observed
in the respective episode, and that propagation scales with the evidence
available beforehand. Event-locked analyses show that all groups detect and
correct for a transition immediately, but only explicitly instructed
participants retain the correction over subsequent trials. Computationally, the
behaviour of 91% of participants is best explained by a latent-state inference
model, and gradual-tracking accounts are rejected for every participant.
Internalizing symptom load does not predict structural inference directly, but
modulates it specifically where structure is manipulated, tracks
transition-specific updating, and robustly predicts the affective experience of
the task.
RQ1 - Does structural uncertainty shift learning from gradual updating toward latent-structure inference?

Deeper instruction produces not only more accurate but more committed responses,
i.e. lower momentary uncertainty in the placement itself.

A single observed transition is propagated to the untested cue, and the
propagation scales with instruction depth.

The absolute cross-cue
generalization index falls by 18.3° across the instruction gradient
(t(66) = −3.25, p = 0.0018; M5), the binary formulation agrees
(β = +0.668 log-odds, z = 2.55, p = 0.011; M5b).

The propagation also scales with the evidence available beforehand.

Participants with more C1 observations before the first C2 trial in the same episode generalize more
completely (β = −6.07°, p = 0.036 in M5; β = +0.300 log-odds, p = 0.023 in M5b).
This provides evidence that the structural representation is acquired
from experience, with observations for one cue carrying over to the second cue through latent structure representation.

Instruction depth improves accuracy, performance and commitment/ net placement concentration,
and it does so by shaping the representation participants work from: a latent
state that is inferred from accumulating evidence and transferred to a cue on
which it was not yet observed.

Both event types displace behaviour equivalently, with angular error rising to
approximately 110–115° at the event trial (oddball, episode transition, each +1) in every condition, consistent with
the 120° shift of the outcome, while conditions differ in the level from
which they depart and to which they return (pre-event baselines approximately
61°, 50° and 35°).
Instructed structure affects retention of the correction.

After a transition, every condition corrects sharply on the following trial
(t1 − t2: C1 0.432, p = 1.0 x 10⁻⁴; C2 0.354, p = 4.0 x 10⁻⁴; C3 0.625,
p < 10⁻⁴), and the immediate correction shows no condition gradient (β = 0.193,
p = 0.29). Total recovery across the window does show a gradient (t1 − t3 x
condition linear β = 0.493, SE 0.182, t = 2.70, p = 0.0070; reproduced in the
stacked model, β = 0.494, p = 0.0084): C1 and C2 end the window where they
started (t1 − t3 = 0.103 and 0.118, both n.s.) whereas C3 sustains the
correction (0.596, p < 10⁻⁴). On the raw scale, C1 falls from roughly 53° to 34°
and returns to 48°, against 25° --> 13° --> 13° in C3 (M2).

Recovery after an oddball is monotonic, with a weaker gradient.

Total
recovery is 0.256 (C1, p = 0.011), 0.319 (C2, p = 0.0006) and 0.542 (C3,
p = 1.4 x 10⁻⁴); the instruction gradient is positive but unresolved (β = 0.286,
p = 0.089 in M4b; β = 0.320, p = 0.060 stacked). The transition and oddball
gradients are not reliably different (difference ≈ 0.17 against SEs of
0.17–0.19).

Transferring the corrected state to the other cue is costly, and equally so in
every condition.

The first appearance of a cue after an event carries higher
error than a repeat appearance: +0.882 log units after a transition
(t(1356) = 12.58, p < 2 x 10⁻¹⁶) and +0.553 after an oddball (t(2016) = 6.95,
p = 4.9 x 10⁻¹²). The effect does not vary by instruction depth (transitions
β = 0.068, p = 0.51; oddballs β = 0.092, p = 0.36). This is an (partly) independent,
trial-level measurement of incomplete cross-cue generalization and converges
with M5/M5b.
The group difference lies in continued refinement.

Restricting
to repeat appearances of the same cue, error continues to fall from the second
to the third post-event trial in C3 (−0.398, p = 0.025) but not in C1 (−0.044)
or C2 (+0.021); the condition interaction is unresolved (β = −0.354, p = 0.12).
The apparent rebound at the third trial is therefore substantially
compositional - later trials contain more first appearances of the other cue
(C1: 116 of 192 versus 55 of 192 at the second trial) - and what distinguishes
explicitly instructed participants is that they keep improving on repeated
exposure/ accumulate evidence rather than plateauing.
Descriptive: reaction magnitude reverses across conditions.

Relative to each
participant’s local pre-event movement, the reaction to an oddball exceeds the
reaction to a transition in C1 (approximately +18° versus +6°), the two are
comparable in C2 (+11° versus +9°), and the ordering reverses in C3 (+15° versus
+24°). This provides descriptive evidence that participants without instructed
structure react more to noise than to genuine change, while those with it react more
to genuine change. The corresponding trial-level interaction in M4a is not

significant (event x condition: oddball β = 0.295, p = 0.11; transition β = 0.352,
p = 0.12), and the difference between
them is negligible (0.057 against an SE of approximately 0.22), so that
specification will not resolve the pattern at any realistic sample size. IMO a
participant-level difference-in-differences on the local baseline, tested as a
single linear contrast, would be the appropriate test but I didn’t run it yet.

The first post-event trial is, by construction, always the first appearance of
its cue (100% in all frames), whereas later trials contain both color cues.
Cue appearance and time since the event are therefore partially
confounded, and the cue-appearance effect is identified only from later trials.
The recovery models carry no cue-appearance term, so their marginal means track
the observed data; the cue-appearance effect is estimated in a separate model
with marginal means averaged over observed cell frequencies. Recovery profiles
for cue appearance would require extrapolation at the first trial, which does not really make sense.

The by-participant recovery slope is dropped from the recovery models because
a 3-trial window cannot support it, retaining it produced boundary fits (obviously).
Under the revised specification M2 and M4b are no longer
singular (M4b: participant SD 0.350, participant:episode SD 0.378, conditional
R² = 0.233). M1, M4a and M_SL2 remain singular on by-participant slopes at their
variance boundary.

children.value: RQ2 - Is internalizing symptom load associated with structural inference, and is that association moderated by instructed structure?

children.label: RQ2 - Is internalizing symptom load associated with structural inference, and is that association moderated by instructed structure?

children.value:
There is no direct association between symptom load and structural
inference.

No trait–behaviour main effect survives FDR correction, and point
estimates for the structural markers are near zero (cue-dissociation rate with
STICSA-T r = −0.069, with IU r = −0.026). Model-derived belief uncertainty is
uncorrelated with the internalizing composite (|r| < 0.01 for all three trace
summaries, all p > 0.98).
The associations that exist are conditional on the manipulation.

Trait x
instruction-depth interactions on cue-dissociation form a uniformly signed family
across six scales: IU-prospective β = −0.62 (p = 0.018), ERS β = −0.61
(p = 0.010), IU-total β = −0.55 (p = 0.022), EAT β = −0.42, IU-inhibitory
β = −0.35, OCI β = −0.29. Individual differences in uncertainty-related traits
express themselves specifically where structure is manipulated, and on the
marker central to RQ1.
Symptom load predicts the affective experience of the task.

Internalizing
load correlates with mean state valence at r = −0.396 (p = 0.0011, q = 0.020),
the only association in this research question surviving correction. It is broad
across uncertainty-relevant scales (ERS r = −0.44, IU r = −0.33, BDI r = −0.33)
and discriminant-valid (mean |r| 0.19 for uncertainty-core versus 0.08 for
discriminant scales). Behaviour is coupled to momentary affect (frustration with
defense rate r = −0.42, p = 3 x 10⁻⁴) but not to trait scores, so no mediated
trait --> behaviour pathway is supported.

Symptom load does not predict how well participants infer
structure. It predicts how the task feels, and it modifies the degree to which
instructed structure translates into structural generalisation. The interaction
family is consistent in direction across six scales; none survives correction at
the present sample size, and all are reported as unresolved.

A third family is specific to transitions and consistently signed. Higher
symptom load is associated with larger post-transition updating (STICSA-T with
transition recovery β = +0.22, p = 0.079; BDI β = +0.22; STICSA-state β = +0.22;
ERS with the post-transition Rule-1 marker β = +0.28, p = 0.026) and with the
structure-learning index level (STICSA-T β = +0.22, OCI β = +0.24, IU β = +0.19).
The oddball side carries the opposite sign (IU β = −0.23, OCI β = −0.29 with
oddball reactivity). Feature-level analyses agree: STICSA-state, STICSA-T and
IU-inhibitory load positively on first-trial post-transition error
(r = 0.26–0.36).
Higher internalizing load is therefore associated with a

separation of
genuine structural change from outcome noise, not a weaker one.

A second cluster links state and cognitive anxiety to higher net entropy
(β = +0.27, p = 0.029) and lower stacking (r = −0.33): less concentrated
allocations on a given trial, i.e. higher momentary uncertainty. This appears in
the behavioural allocation measures but not in model-derived belief uncertainty,
so the two dissociate.
the following paragraph is a mediocre draft - written spontaneously and not good, but kept as a starting point

Trait anxiety and related constructs (as well as internalizing symptoms more broadly, see below) show no significant main-effect relationship with structural inference. Nonetheless, the descriptive effects build a coherent set of condition-dependent and transition-specific associations that converge across scales and analyses. The clearest is a large, uniformly-signed family of trait x instruction-depth interactions on cue-dissociation (IU-prospective β=−0.62, ERS −0.61, IU-total −0.55, plus EAT, IU-inhibitory, OCI same-signed), suggesting that the structural-generalization benefit of deeper instruction is systematically modulated by uncertainty-/internalizing-related traits, i.e. individual differences express themselves specifically where structure is manipulated. A second group of descriptive effects links (state/cognitive) anxiety to higher net-placement entropy (and lower stacking) (β≈+0.27). Interpreted cautiously, high anxiety individuals may thus infer higher local stochasiticity compared to individuals with low-to-medium anxiety. This converges with earlier evidence from tasks in which individuals learn to distinguish between volatility and stochasticity, where high trait anxiety was assocated with an overestimation of stochasticity and an underestimation of volatility (cite). Crucially, this was commonly interpreted as reduced or even affected learning (cite). Our results provide an alternative interpretation: while outcome variability within stable latent states is more readily attributed to stochastic noise, thereby decreasing sensitivity to volatility as long as this volatility does not arise from a specific hidden structure, reactivity to structured variablility of the generative structure itself (i.e. state transitions) is increased while sensitivity to stochasiticity at this structure-level is decreased. This is not consistent with generally altered/ reduced learning but with a different focus on

should be learned. It is further consistent with evidence demonstrating, that high anxiety individuals have a higher tendency to infer and rely on (hidden) structures in the context of latent state inference (Zika et al., 2023). A higher structural prior / more pronouced expectation that dynamics are driven by switches between discrete states rather than continuous gradual dynamics would give rise to a “misatribution” of volatility to stochasticity as long as the observed variablility through volatility is not distinguishable from local within-state stochasticity (actually a higher tolerance for local noise, in order to stick with model that provides a structured explanation for the observed dynamics, thereby allowing for straightforward action selection - otherwise, the uncertainty about the model generating outcomes would have to increase rapidly). But as soon as volatility is governed by a certain hidden structure that can be identified, this “misattribution” diminishes. Instead, high-anxiety/ internalizing idividuals show a relatively “better” structural inference compared to individuals with lower anxiety/internalizing symptom load.

A third, smaller but convergent cluster (β≈+0.2 across SLI level, transition-recovery, and post-transition update, with the opposite sign for oddball reactivity) suggests higher internalizing goes with sharper, not weaker, structure-vs-noise dissociation - descriptively consistent with anxiety accelerating structural learning. None survive FDR at N=65 (which detects only r>=0.34), but their magnitude and cross-analysis convergence provide preliminary evidence .... .
M_SL3: STICSA-T --> transition_recovery_mean β=+0.22, p=0.079; BDI +0.22, p=0.081; STICSA-state +0.22, p=0.072. Three internalizing scales, same sign, all ~0.22
M_SL3: STICSA-T --> SLI level β=+0.22, p=0.08; OCI +0.24; IU +0.19; IU-inhibitory +0.21. Again a same-signed family around +0.2
two-stage: ERS --> rule1_marker_delta_post_transition β=+0.28, p=0.026 (largest single main effect in the whole grid)

This pattern of effects suggests that higher internalizing symptom load is associated with larger post-transition belief updates, stronger transition-recovery and a (marginally) higher structure-learning index. The sign is positive throughout, consistent with the hypothesis that anxiety may

structure learning. Moreover, this pattern is specifically about transitions (genuine structural change), not about oddballs (noise). For oddballs, the direction of the effect is reversed and weaker (oddball_reactivity x IU β=−0.23, x OCI −0.29), suggesting that higher internalizing symptom load is associated with less oddball reactivity. Together, the present pattern of descriptive effects, i.e. that individuals with higher internalizing symptom load show an increased adaptivity to (hidden) structural change combined with a simultaneously reduced reactivity to oddballs (structure-level stochasticity), suggests that higher-internalizing individuals show a sharper structure-vs-noise dissociation.

Together, these results challenge the view that anxiety may affect learning. Instead they suggest that hgih anxiety individuals may have a higher sensitivity to hidden structures/ patterns that are not directly observable (obscured by noise) but carry a predictive value if inferred correctly.

No trait x structure x condition three-way interaction survives FDR correction
(all q ≥ 0.45). Condition-stratified correlations rest on 13–30 participants per
cell and are hypothesis-generating only.
RQ3 - Do the model parameters recover their behavioural signatures, and do they carry the symptom associations?

children.label: RQ3 - Do the model parameters recover their behavioural signatures, and do they carry the symptom associations?

children.value:
Latent-state inference is the winning account, while gradual tracking is
rejected outright.

The structural model is the best-fitting model for 62 of 68
participants (91%), with a mean posterior model probability of 0.91. Both
gradual-tracking models win zero participants and have mean posterior
probability 0.00. Because the tracking models are the formal expression of the
gradual-learning alternative, this is the most direct available evidence for the RQ1
hypothesis.
The parameters are calibrated and, with one exception, well recovered.

Simulation-based calibration returns near-uniform rank histograms (rank means
467–503 of 1000 for five of six parameters). Recovery correlations are 0.996
(precision weighting), 0.985 (placement noise), 0.934 (cue sensitivity), 0.910
(belief momentum), 0.825 (perceived volatility) and 0.636 (noise reactivity).
The parameters measure what they were constructed to measure.

Pre-specified
convergent-validity pairings hold for the well-recovered parameters: precision
weighting with net entropy (r = −0.87, p = 5 x 10⁻²²) and stacking (r = +0.62),
cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset (r = +0.81, p = 9 x 10⁻¹⁷), and
belief momentum with post-transition belief revision (r = −0.42, p = 4 x 10⁻⁴),
all Holm-significant within family.

The computational model is identifiable, calibrated and valid
against the behavioural measures it indexes, and it selects structural inference
over gradual tracking essentially unanimously.

No trait–parameter association survives FDR correction (yet?), and no mediation path
reaches significance, as expected when both constituent paths are of the order
r = 0.3 at N = 65.

Posterior predictive checks reproduce most behavioural signatures (spontaneous
switch rate 75% coverage; large-shift rate and oddball-follow rate approximately
68%), without a coverage area bias (the CIs are fairly tight, so that the absolute deviation remains practically negligible). Belief lability was not reproduced (16% coverage, observed exceeding
predicted in 57 of 68 participants), nor fully are within-state placement
variance and oddball angular shift (the latter two features are sufficiently close though).
The reason for this pattern is that the model cannot jump as fast as participants do - I’m still trying to find a solution for this but IMO even the current version captures participant behavior very well. These differences are genuinely really hard to recognize in the net placement heatmaps (participant behavior vs model behavior, replayed with the participant’s inferred parameters). Here a few examples:

Noise reactivity is the least identifiable parameter (recovery r = 0.64,
reliability ≈ 0.41). Diagnostic work established that this is a property of the
forward model rather than of the estimation method: an independent supervised
learner trained on the same summary features reproduces the recovery profile of
the neural estimator to two decimal places, and the parameter’s behavioural
channels are suppressed downstream (the learning gate saturates at κ = 4 with a
120° displacement, and the predictive mixture component is removed by the
commitment sharpening before net allocation). A two-stage allocation reserving
round(7 x ρ_eff) nets for the oddball location raises the ceiling from 0.60 to
0.92 in simulation, at a cost of 0.09 for perceived volatility, leaving switching
behaviour unchanged. The model has been patched and awaits retraining and
posterior predictive re-validation (just didn’t find the time yet - this is retraining No.9 (?) and the training has to run over night). Until then, results involving noise reactivity, including the absence of the predicted association with trait
anxiety, are limited by identifiability rather than evidence of absence.
Nevertheless, different noise reactivity values produce exactly the expected model behavior:

The transition-versus-oddball distinction is where the three questions come together. RQ1
establishes that instructed structure changes what is propagated across cues and
retained across trials, and that propagation scales with prior evidence. RQ3
establishes that the generative account is latent-state inference rather than
gradual tracking, and that belief momentum indexes post-transition revision. RQ2
places internalizing load on the same axis: larger post-transition updating,
lower oddball reactivity and lower belief momentum, observed consistently at the
behavioural, parameter and symptom levels, though no individual association is
resolved at the present sample size.

The following selection is a preliminary suggestion for which analyses to focus on because they are load bearing for the core results outlined above; supporting analyses can qualify or corroborate them ofc.
Instruction depth improves performance and commitment
Structure is inferred and transferred, and is evidence-dependent
Instruction affects retention, not reaction speed
M2 planned contrasts (t1 − t3 x condition)
The generative process is latent-state inference
Model comparison; SBC and recovery; Level-B convergent validity
Symptom load modulates structure where it is manipulated, and tracks affect
Two-stage trait x condition; M_SL3 transition family; trait–parameter partial correlations; internalizing --> state valence
Supporting, for supplementary material (this is just a note for myself):

M4a, M4b, M6, the B-series
event-versus-baseline models (which belong to Oscars eye-tracking work), M_SL1 and M_SL2, the stacked recovery
dissociation, the transfer-versus-consolidation models, the direction-asymmetry
contrasts, the Level-A parameter–feature grid, the hierarchical trait models (as
an explicit methodological caution), and the oddball diagnostics.
